utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. Barney Thomas, Carmela Javier, and Dan Saxon for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, Tina Drolec, and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before I call you, Mr. Lukic, just to find out from Madam stenographer, I see there isn't any of your colleagues outside. Can we go on? Thank you. THE COURT REPORTER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. We're going to continue where we left off two days ago, and now I'd like to give you a binder with the documents that we are going to work on. I have already shown that to my learned friends from the Prosecution, so we can immediately pass it on to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have on our screens again Defence document 01113D page 12 in B/C/S and page 16 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, that's the rule of responsibilities that we already saw. Can you please move to Article 26, which is on page 19 in your hard copy. We'll go back to the subject that we left off when we suspended your examination. Can you just give me -- we discussed the subject of material and market inspection. You have given us some general answers concerning this organisational unit of the Ministry of Defence. You remember that this is where we left off. You gave us a general comment on Article 26. Now, as a follow-up and in order to finish this subject and this document, I would kindly ask you to comment on item 1 which reads that: "This financial and market inspection controls the drafting and the implementation of the budget of the Yugoslav Army, the harmonisation of the budget with the plans for development, building, and equipping the Yugoslav Army and the efficient use of the budget funds in the units and installations of the Yugoslav Army." Can you tell us how that inspection operated specifically with regard to these tasks?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The financial market inspection is an organ of the Federal Ministry of Defence. As you said it yourself, its responsibility is to carry out tasks entrusted to it as their responsibility. Based on these rules and other laws that pertain to the responsibility of the MOD, what it stems from here, it means that it oversees the entire financial and material operations of all organisational units of the MOD and the Yugoslav Army. The focus here is on financial inspection and control of the budget. The budget is being prepared in order to be adopted by the highest authority in the country, which is the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 2 says that this controls the expenditure of budget funds for each purpose. My question is: Who is it that defines the purposes of the budget, and can you enumerate them?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When proposing a budget, the General Staff of the VJ, at the request of the Ministry of Defence, more precisely the administration for finances and budget of the federal MOD, requests the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to put down their requirements with regard to assets that have to be included in the budget according to specify purposes. These proposals put together with the proposals coming from organisational units of the Ministry of Defence are then submitted to the minister of defence for approval. If the minister of defence endorses these proposals, then a follow-up procedure is implemented. These kind of proposal is then submitted to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me an additional explanation. You asked me who decides the purposes and who approves the plan. That is actually the next stage after the budget has been adopted by the Federal Assembly. Then the responsible department of the federal government, in this particular case the Ministry of Defence, adopts a plan specifying the purposes of the use of budget. In this particular interest, the General Staff of the VJ has no influence any longer on the amount of budget and the purposes provided this has been verified by the Assembly and the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on we shall come back to the budget again. Can you please comment on Article 8. It says that this administration --

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 8, and it says that this administration oversees the expenditure, budget expenditures. Can you tell me who submits reports on the expenditure?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expenditure reports relating to the budget on behalf of organisational units, the General Staff of the VJ is submitted by the 5th Administration of the General Staff of the VJ pertaining to the General Staff, and as for other organisational units of the units, the officials or the heads of these organisational units of the Ministry of Defence do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've finished with this document, and I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given a exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this shall be assigned Exhibit D240.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at another document which is the Law on Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Can we please have P1183, page 4 in the B/C/S and page 6 in English, and the specific articles that I would like you to look at, sir, are first Article 42. Can you just give me a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We are going to enlarge Article 42, which relates to the federal government. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government. Article 42? Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us just in few words what is the essence of the Law on Defence, what it governs, and what kind of provisions it contains.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is one of the series of laws adopted on the basis of the constitution of the FRY of the 27th April 1992. It is a precursor of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. In this particular article, 42, all the obligations have been set out very precisely, including the tasks of the federal government. What is important for the Army of Yugoslavia and the ministry is contained under Item 1 of this article which says that the federal government shall implement federal laws and other regulations adopted by the Federal Assembly that relate to the country's defence. There's a particular item that refers to the Army of Yugoslavia, which is item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This law is self-explanatory, as well as the provisions. Can you please comment item 6 because it is related to the topic that we have been discussing. Can you tell us what are the responsibilities of the federal government when it comes to material and finance funds mentioned under item 6.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, responsibilities of the General Staff and the federal government of the FRY are separated here, and it is precisely set out in item 6 which says that it is in charge of securing required material and financial resources for implementing the country's defence plan and securing the federal commodity reserves for the country's needs in case of a war, an imminent threat of war or state of emergency, as well as for financing other aspects which are of particular importance for the country's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look at Article 43. I'm not going to ask you to make particular analysis of this article which speaks about the responsibilities of the MOD, except that I would like to as you to give us an example relating to this introductory paragraph and explain to us what does it mean when it says here: "The Federal Minister of Defence performs the following administrative and specialist tasks relating to the implementation of the country's defence policy." What does that mean specifically?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 43 defines the tasks and obligations of the Ministry of Defence that relate to the implementation of the defence policy. When we speak about administrative and specialist tasks, administrative means that the minister of defence, as the person in charge of the ministry, is entitled to adopt all kinds of enactments, orders and decisions relating to the implementation of the defence policy; whereas professional specialty tasks means that organisational units of the same ministry within their purview of the ministry make proposals for certain enactments, documents, and rules and regulation to be adopted and which are required to fulfil all the obligations that are within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just comment Article 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for your benefit, it's at the end of the page that we see now, and it goes on to page 7, but I think what we see on this particular page will be sufficient, and I would like the witness to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, Article 44 speaks about inspection that we already discussed when we spoke about organisational units. I am particular interested in hearing your comment on item 2 which reads: "The implementation of decisions and enactments rendered by the President of the Republic, the Supreme Defence Council and the federal government."

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 44 of this Law on Defence explicitly provides for the Federal Ministry of Defence, in addition to its other duties and responsibilities, that it is obliged to implement the decisions and enactments rendered by the president of the republic, the Supreme Defence Council, and the federal government. That means that the highest authority or the organ of command and control, which is the Supreme Defence Council and whose obligations are set out by the constitution, this implies that its duty is to implement them to the letter. This also relates to the decisions taken by the federal government, which means if the president of the republic based -- adopted a decision based on the decision adopted by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let us just be more accurate. Pursuant to this article, if the Supreme Defence Council and the Commander-in-Chief adopts a certain decision, who is in charge of overseeing the implementation of that decision and to whom they send notice if any notice is required to be sent with regard to the implementation?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago we spoke about the inspection, but we only focused on one aspect, which was financial and market inspections. Here we are talking about the jurisdiction of the administration for civilian defence, which says that everything that this administration for civilian defence does and the documents that it prepares for the federal government, it is the Ministry of Defence that carries out inspection to check whether the enactments and laws relating to the defence of the country are being implemented in line with the law and the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if they find out that the Supreme Defence Council's decision or the decisions of the Commander-in-Chief are not being implemented as provided, what shall it do?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inspection in charge of the Federal Ministry of Defence, if in the course of inspection and control finds out that there has been a breach of law or that the decision of the Supreme Defence Council has been violated, they submit their report to the minister of defence as the person in charge to instigate certain measures as provided by the law. Which particular measures are going to be taken depends on the decision of the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just ask, who are the "they" that are referred to in the question and answer at this point? The question reads: "And if they find out that." Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the witness's previous answer where he mentioned the inspection service of the Ministry of Defence which he called the civilian -- but let us have the witness tell us this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the inspection service of defence is directly subordinated to the minister of defence. It is made up of three, actually, inspection units: The civilian defence inspection unit, the civil engineering and construction inspection unit, and the financial and market inspection unit. Here we are talking particular about -- particularly about the civilian defence inspection unit, because this is within their remit. And as I said, this is part of the inspection department as one of the ministry's departments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you said this is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said this department makes its inspections, and at page 9, lines 8 to 9, you say they submit their report to the minister of defence as the person in charge to instigate certain measures as provided by the law. And what then does the minister do once that investigation has been done with the results of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when a report is submitted to the defence minister, and when one reviews all of the problems of what nature, what the degree of responsibility entailed might be, what the subject matter is, he will then decide whether this is something that belongs to his area of work and whether he has the powers to conclude whether it is possible that certain areas, in certain sectoral units can be remedied swiftly and with no consequences. He then adopts a decision and sets deadlines for these areas to be remedied. If there is any sort of responsibility involved, in the sense of violations of certain laws and regulations, the minister then takes other measures that are available under the prevailing laws. This can be criminal responsibility. This can be material responsibility, or other types of liability regulated by all these specific laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand you, and I'm going to put a scenario to you, and I would like you to tell me whether it is correct or incorrect. Earlier I thought you said that the Ministry of Defence implements orders from the SDC, from the president, and from the federal government; am I right thus far? Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if in I am pleating those orders this is these violations of laws, is it your testimony that neither the president nor the Supreme Defence Council, nor the federal government have supervisory powers over the Ministry of Defence, that the Ministry of Defence will then have to supervise itself through this department that conducts the investigation, make a report to the minister, and the minister will decide whether the results are within his jurisdiction or whether he must pass them on to somebody else. There is nobody who supervises the minister? Is that your testimony? Do I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your question merits an additional explanation. If I may, I will try to explain. What we're looking at here is this: It's not about the fact that there is no other form of supervision above the minister. The minister answers to the prime minister, that is, the federal government. The federal government, depending on the sector in question, are we talking about finances, are we talking about other types of decisions, are we talking about material violations, has its own financial supervision or control. Likewise, these decisions or responsibilities of the defence minister go through the federal government and all the way to the Federal Assembly. The Federal Assembly is the supreme legislative body. There are certain committees that are part of the Federal Assembly such as the budget control committee, as well as safety and protection committee. Depending on the sector, the appropriate federal bodies do this on behalf of the prime minister, and the government in its turn is supervised or, if you like, under the control of the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, do you know if the federal defence minister was involved in the work of the Supreme Defence Council? Did you have any direct first-hand knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the defence minister is not a member of the Supreme Defence Council. Nevertheless, when matters of exceptional importance are reviewed from the domain of the federal government's work and the appropriate ministry, the defence minister takes part in the work of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another document that I would like us to look at just to round this off. This is a Defence exhibit, D114, the Law on Property on the -- of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in keeping with your earlier guidelines, we tendered only a part of this law, not the law in its entirety, and I'm now willing to go through no more than a couple of articles and paragraphs with this witness. For that purpose, we have a draft translation into English of some of these articles and provisions. I would like to ask you, therefore, to follow the draft translation for the articles in question, then once we receive an official translation, it will tender as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just explain something, Mr. Lukic. How come it already has an exhibit number if it's got only a draft translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm happy to explain, Your Honour. We have D114, which is an exhibit. It contains no more than several paragraphs of this law. When we were working with Mr. Starcevic, you instructed us to comment on no more than a couple of paragraphs from one portion of the law. And now we want to go through another couple of articles with this witness, and that's why we have no more than draft translation. We did not have a complete translation. You remember that we criticised this practice earlier on. We do believe that laws should be tendered in their entirety, but the translation service and your guidelines kept us from having the entire law translated, and this also happens to be the case with the Law on Property, the one that I'm dealing with right now. Only a handful of the actual articles have been tendered, and what we are facing now is another set of articles of the same law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it means the articles you are about to deal with do not form part of D114. Then you must give them a 65 ter number, and they will be admitted as a separate exhibit, or you can request that they be added to D114. But you can't -- you can't call them part of 114 if they have been tendered yet. D114 is only those that have been tendered so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The B/C/S is complete, and you are quite right, D114 contains only those articles that have so far been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying to me that D114 in the B/C/S is the complete act, and the English is only translation of certain articles? Can't be that. Shouldn't be that. The English version should be exactly the same as the B/C/S. You can't, you can't tender the whole in the B/C/S and -- and just give a part in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honour. I fully understand what you're saying. Please allow me to just check what exactly the situation is and then we can deal with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you are right. What we have in the B/C/S of D114 is merely a portion of that law and not the law in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to check that with the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe it would be a good idea to take the opportunity during the break to talk to the Registry, and maybe they have a proposal for us on how to tender this document into evidence; but we might either give it a 65 ter number or perhaps just link this up with the existing Exhibit D114, of course as long as Your Honour agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... during the break, Mr. Lukic, but in the future just make sure that what is tendered, the B/C/S is identical to the English, a whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- a part this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try not to further complicate matters. You realise that we have a lot of documents in our 65 ter list that are -- are already parts of some P documents tendered by the OTP. Perhaps the Chamber should think about what they might find useful in their work. Would it be better to have it marked as item 1 of the Law on Property, a part of which is in D114 and now a new number? Personally, I think that it would be much easier for us, for each of us to analyse this later on if we just get an added number for this. This is just my proposal, but maybe I should check later on with the Registry whether that is indeed the most helpful course of action we can take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you are now proposing to deal with with this witness, it's not the balance of the entire act. It's a few other articles of the act. So if you knew you were going to use these articles also, they should have formed part of D114 even though you may not have dealt with them -- with these particular articles at that time, because you might have known that you are going to deal with these with this witness, and they would have then formed one exhibit. Now that that has not happened, I think, and I'm also saying this subject to correction, that it might perhaps be better when finally this is admitted to be made part of D114 so that they are keep at one place, articles of the same act are kept at one place. But I would ask the team to try to ensure that at the first admission of a part, the entire part that is going to be needed is admitted. Then when you refer to that exhibit later, it's already in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir -- Mr. Nikolic, we have this in front of us and the Trial Chamber only has the corresponding articles. Can you tell us the name of this law in front of you and when it was adopted, when it was published? The Chamber also has that in English, I believe.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's called "Decree on adoption of law on the property of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was adopted in 1993 and published in the Official Gazette of the SRJ, number 19, dated the 23rd of July, 1993. The law normally comes into force eight days after its publication. So that's how you should see this in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on Article 2. What is it in relation to, and what sort of property are we talking about, property of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe you are now looking at the draft translation and should be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 2, the Law on Property of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, General, I'm sorry to interrupt. The transcript refers to Article 2, but I have Article 38 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are supposed to have been given a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic should pass --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's what I need, Your Honours. Thank you. My apologies, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Article 2 of the law precisely envisages in paragraph 1 what constitutes the property of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This comprises the possession of things, real estate and movable property, monetary assets, commercial notes and other ownership rights both domestically and foreign whose holder is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Paragraph 2 specifies which bodies are to be considered the federal bodies and services in the sense of this law. The Federal Assembly, the president of the republic, the federal government, the federal ministries, the Federal Court, the federal state prosecutor, the national bank of Yugoslavia, the federal constitutional courts and the other federal bodies as envisaged in this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of Article 1 tells us about these monetary funds. Can you please now comment on Article 40. I believe you should have that in front of you, sir. Article 40, please.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monetary assets. Article 40 defines these monetary assets. It says that these are assets secured by the federal budget for the purpose of financing the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its operations. All of this has to be in keeping with the federal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the salaries? Are the salaries, too, part of the budget, and are they part of these monetary assets?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move on to Article 45. It's on the same page, I believe, in the draft translation.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm expecting your answer.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 45 of this law talks about the supervision of the implementation of the enactments of this law and other federal laws relative to the acquisition, use, management, and dispensation of FRY property. This links up with Article 7 or refers to Article 7. As far as I know, Article 7 refers to the Federal Justice Ministry. But if I may just provide an additional explanation, please. The law provides for the fact that the Federal Justice Ministry does not have this sort of power over the federal defence ministry. Rather, it's the minister with his inspections which is something that we covered a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've been looking at this document now and I would like to mark it with the 65 ter number 03321D. I move that the document be MFI'd for the time being, and once we have received a complete translation, we shall see what course of action is best taken with documents such as this one that were provisionally MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry. Document 03321D is admitted into evidence, marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it looks like this is causing serious problems within the -- within Registry, and is it possible for you to tender this once we have got the official translation? Then it can become straight part of D114 at that stage rather than give it a separate 65 ter number and a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fantastic. Thank you, Your Honour. I think that proposal is great, and that's precisely the course of action that I will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to more specific matters, General, which is something that we mentioned two days ago, but let's try to talk about the salaries and get to the gist of it, fringe benefits for the Federal Army of Yugoslavia under the existing laws. Can we please move on to the law on the army, which is an exhibit, P197. Article 71. In the B/C/S it's page 7, and in the English it's pages 17 and 18. Article 71. May we please have a look. Sir, what salaries are there? What forms do these salaries take, or what is the basis for these salaries for members of the Army of Yugoslavia? Hold on a second, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is at the bottom of the page. It's exactly the right portion in English, the one that we have on our screens now. Article 71, paragraph 1. This will be perfect for you to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What makes up the salary of a professional member of the VJ? That is specifically envisaged in Article 71 of the law on the VJ. What we find here is the elements of the salary. By the same token, the salaries of the professional members of the VJ comprise a part of the salary as defined by the rank, a part of the salary as defined by the relative position of this member within the VJ, a military supplement, which is also part of the salary, and there is another part of the salary that may or may not be due on account of a particular position that a member holds within the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of these elements, were the salaries calculated for each and every member of the VJ based on these criteria?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, regarding the way the salaries were calculated and paid, more specific standards are to be found in the decree on the salaries of the professional members of the VJ. And this was a document adopted by the federal government. What follows, based on all of that, is that the salaries of the professional members of the VJ were different in terms of the actual amounts in terms of how high the salaries were. Those were the higher rank that were a more important duty. Those closer to their retirement age or those occupying a particularly important position would, as a rule, have higher salaries. For that to be codified and made into a law, one needed to have certain legal documents first. So this decree now regulates that. It's the order on the establishment of a certain individual, the assignment of a certain individuals to a certain establishment post within the system, and this position is defined exactly under the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us try to illustrate this in the most graphic manner possible. Given the rank system, I thin that should be pretty clear, nevertheless; for example, we have a colonel who works at the military institute for geography. Does this person have the same salary as the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. You said, "Does this person have the same salary as the," and the sentence is not finished but the witness has answered, he said, No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So does he have the same salary as a colonel who works as the chief of the first administration of the sector for operations and staff affairs of the General Staff of the VJ. By way of example, yesterday, rather a few days ago, oh, yes, we had General Simic, who was lieutenant-colonel at the time, meaning we want to know about his salary, and for example, another colonel who is, as I said by way of an example, worked in an institute or something like that.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this requires some more detailed explanation. In order to understand better the reasons for this, we should refer to this fourth element of the salary when I was explaining the components of salary. The director of the military geographical institute, for example, holds a different position, has different tasks, physical and mental, and also different responsibilities as compared to the head of the administration or deputy head of administration in an operational administration. This allowance expressed in percentage varies. For example, in one case it would be 15 per cent of the basic salary, and that would apply to the director of the military geographical institute; whereas the person employed in the first administration, this percentage would be, for example, 20 per cent. Similarly, as per establishment, we have post-related groups although we have personnel with same ranks. It nevertheless means that according to establishment in the military geographical institute, a colonel working there would be in post-related group number 9. Those working in the first administration would be in post-related group number 7, and pursuant to that, he would receive a higher allowance. I hope this was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think so. Now, do we also have the length of service as one of the elements that affect the pay as mentioned in the law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that self explanatory?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We said that the military allowances provided in Article 74 and the law is very precise in that respect. Can you tell us what the annual vacation allowance is? Is that another fringe benefit that -- or entitlement? Where it is mentioned in the law?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period when this law on the VJ army was in force, there was certain remuneration or the so-called annual leave allowance was provided, and that was one of the fringe benefits payable to the personnel. This was governed by the federal government decree on salaries and other fringe benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we please look at Article 211, page 53 in English, page 18 in B/C/S. What kind of benefits derive from the status of members of the personnel with respect to social security and other forms of insurance and security provisions?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can you tell us what kind of social security are provided for military personnel under the law?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on the Yugoslav Army, there is an area which we call area number 3 of the law on the army and that relates to social security issues. It is made up of three elements: Health insurance, pension, and disability insurance. Since you mentioned Article 201, it regulates health insurance of military personnel, military academy cadets, students of secondary military school, trainees of reserve officer schools and individuals in the reserve forces. Now, from Article 217 onwards, we have health protection issues and provisions of professional soldiers, commissioned and non-commissioned officers, contract soldiers and military personnel in retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are the rights that the families of military personnel enjoy with regard to this protection? Can we look at Article 216. Do family members enjoy certain benefits from the status of the member of the military?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 216 of this law provides full protection, health insurance of family members of professional or personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the family.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said all members of the family of the military personnel who has this kind of insurance. I tried to explain this in a more graphic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in a couple of words about another entitlement that stems from the status, and that's the housing support and insurance. What kind of rights derive from this particular provision?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provision of housing facilities includes providing housing for persons by allocating flats to them from the housing stock of the then JNA and now the VJ or by granting housing credit lines through banks or by allocating a service flat to be used for a period of time while the member of the personnel is serving and carrying out his duty, which means that for the duration of his service he needs to have a housing facility provided for both him and members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can we please explain a notion that probably is a bit foreign to the Trial Chamber because it's a relic from the self-management era. When we talk about tenancy right, can you tell us what that was, and what happened when these tenancy rights were converted into ownership rights and how this affected certain groups of citizens?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on housing construction and provision of housing facilities that were in force until the Law on Property was adopted, one of the provisions related to tenancy rights. Now, what tenancy rights mean. Tenancy rights involving allocating a flat to a certain person from the JNA housing stock or later of the VJ housing stock without the right to acquire an ownership right on this particular flat. However, according to the regulations then in force, there was a possibility which was conditioned for the person involved to have spent 15 or more years in the service to lease this apartment for an indefinite period of time and with eventually a possibility for him to buy it and to convert it into his private property.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know in the former SFRY and the FRY when these regulations relating to the buying off of flats, was that going on? What was the actual market value of the flats, and what was the amounts that were indeed paid by those who were using them, because I think there was a discrepancy between these two values.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation relating to the housing issues during the period of the SFRY was such that the JNA had exceptional possibilities to quickly resolve all the housing problems of the personnel. Since I was head of the sector for housing in the JNA, that is to say in the third department of the then personnel administration, which was later renamed to administration for status-related issues, based on some statistical data the average time for a member of the army who was waiting to be allocated a flat was two years. At the time, people started buying off the flats on which they had tenancy rights, and they became owners eventually. And we are talking about a large number of people. These people finally decided that after the termination of service, for a variety of reasons, education of their children, et cetera, wanted to remain in these flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe I wasn't accurate enough. Let me put it this way: At the time when these flats were bought during this enormous inflation, how did people actually pay for them, and why this buying of flats was relatively easy in that period?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flats from the housing stock of the JNA, as I said before, were bought off just like any other flat in society. The principles and the instalments relating to payment did not differ from other arrangements in other segments of society. As for the value of the flat, for some it was very small, but for others it was very high. It all depended on the length of service. If you allow me, I have to clarify further. There was a special law called the law on earmarking funds for housing construction. If I'm not wrong, it was adopted in 1974. Under this law, all members of the JNA were obliged to earmark 4.5 per cent of their gross salary for housing construction irrespective of whether they already had a flat or didn't have a flat at all. This was based on the principle of solidarity. Thanks to that, enormous funds were accumulated and that provided swift solutions for housing problems of the military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The day before yesterday, you mentioned another article, i.e., Article 87. Page 21 in English, Your Honours, and page 8 in B/C/S. General, can you just briefly comment this article, because you referred to it the day before yesterday when you talked about who decided the salaries.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this article is the last one that relates to the military salaries, Article 87 gives federal government the responsibility to -- what they're going to be deciding on and what is going to be deciding by the minister of defence. What this shows is that the federal government shall prescribe the salary according to the rank --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read it.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military allowance, et cetera. Let me just explain. When I spoke about different segments of salary, I didn't mention this segment relating to the length of service, and it is decided according to the republican provisions. It is calculated .5 per cent per each year of service, but it cannot exceed the total percentage of 20. I thought this would be a helpful explanation for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a good time for us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I keep saying that we are finished with the legal part, but we are not. There is one more article I would like the witness to comment on, and then we will be moving on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, that's Article 337 of the Law on Army of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 88 of Exhibit 197. Article 337 is the one I should like Mr. Nikolic to look at. Page 30 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I believe that we have already discussed this, but tell me, does this article define the matters we discussed today and two days ago as part of the provisions covered by the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness's microphones please be switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer, please, Mr. Nikolic, now that the microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is connected to Article 337 of the Law on Property that we discussed a moment ago. Here the manner in which funds and material assets are to be managed and dispensed is defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two days ago you mentioned the Law on Finances of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We don't have that piece of legislation, unfortunately. However, who is it who is in charge of managing assets who is mentioned in the Law on the VJ and in connection with the law on financing of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's called the Law on Finances of the FRY, which places emphasis on assets available, managed and dispensed with. The chief of the staff is not the one who would be entitled to manage these assets. He is entitled to dispense the assets that are conferred upon him pursuant to a decision of the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, General, we will be moving to a different topic. You said on the 27th of April, 1992, the FRY constitution was passed and a new state was formed, as it were. This historic moment, what bearing did it have on the Yugoslav People's Army, in terms of its status and the status of its members?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What became of the Yugoslav People's Army once a new state was set up and a new constitution passed on the 27th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of the 4th of May, 1992, a decision was made whereby all the units of the Yugoslav People's Army were within 15 days to withdraw from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and cross over to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That meant that within 15 days they had to withdraw all the units, including military hardware, troops and families of servicemen. It raised a number of difficult issues as to how to deal with the transportation of men and assets. However, the greatest difficulty faced the families and professional servicemen of the former JNA who remained in the territory of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina and the Republika Srpska and became members, joined the ranks of armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get back to that later. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, there were great difficulties which needed solutions. Primarily the status of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia needed to be resolved as well as any other material and social issues, accommodation, food, disposition, billeting and the related locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us call up a 65 ter document, 476D, an order issued by the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when you say this document is 476D -- okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I skipped the first two zeros.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, according to the date of the decision -- or, rather the date of the decision coincides with the date of the adoption of the FRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 2 of the order signed by Branko Kostic -- well, first of all can you tell us what was the role of Branko Kostic at the time?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the vice-president of the Presidency of the SFRY as the body vested with commanding powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It reads: "The plan should contain the transformation of the JNA into the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its reducing to the territory of the FRY and citizens of the FRY, which implies also a transfer of non-nationals [sic] of FRY who are members of the JNA from the territories of other republics to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and vice versa."

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. There's a discrepancy between the translation and the transcript and the English version of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I seem to have misread this. Page 30, line 12: "Transfer to nationals of FRY," not "non-nationals." So the English translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "transfer to nationals," that doesn't sound grammatically correct. What do you transfer to the nationals?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Transfer of citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Transfer of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of citizens. yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. There's a further inconsistency. If I could just pause the transcript for a moment. At line 30 -- sorry, page 30, line 12, at line -- sorry, page 30, line 11, we have -- and I'm not sure if my learned friend was reading here or whether he was putting a proposition, but what the transcript records is: "The plan should contain the transformation of the JNA into the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its reducing to the territory of the FRY and citizens of the FRY which implies also a transfer of non-nationals." Now, I don't know if at that point he is reading from the provision, because if he was, that's not what the English version of the provision says, which there's no talk of implication at all. It expressly states that it includes the transfer of citizens. And I'm just not clear whether what my learned friend was doing was reading the provision or whether he was commenting on the provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading the text. I wasn't commenting on it, and I don't see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is that what appears on the transcript does not accord with what appears on the -- on Article 2 of the order, and that kind of problem can be solved by counsel not reading a document which is on the screen but ask questions about it, because when you read it, we have it on the screen and then you bring it on the transcript and this kind of problem will arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, rather than me reading the document, can you give us your comments on the text of item 2, and can you tell us what it is that you know about this matter.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is an order issued by the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia following the adoption of the FRY constitution or on the date of its passing, whereby the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the JNA is ordered to fulfil certain obligations within the time limit stated. And item 2 precisely defines that the staff of the Supreme Command should draw up a plan which would provide for the transformation of the JNA into the Army of Yugoslavia since all of the JNA and its component parts should be reduced to the territory of the FRY and the citizens of the FRY. The term that seemed to be the problem here had to do with the transfer onto the citizens of the FRY, because you know that the units were spread out across the SFRY. So those who were in other countries, in other republics then the FRY should return to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the "vice versa" at the end? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain this. This means that those who are not nationals of the FRY can inversely return to the territories or cross over to the territories of their respective republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, or maybe Mr. Nikolic, at page 32, line -- starting from line 14, you say: "The term that seemed to be the problem here had to do with the transfer onto the citizens of the FRY ..." I'm not quite sure I understand what is meant by the term "transfer onto the citizens of the FRY," and I don't seem to see a similar term in Article 2 of the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I can only clarify this one sentence which I believes constitution the problem. It also implies or includes the transfer onto. You can't read it clearly. The citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who are members of the JNA from the territories of other republics, because the JNA, up until that point, had been deployed throughout the territories, and they should be returning to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia where the Army of Yugoslavia would be constituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That I understand. What I don't understand is "transfer onto the citizens," or onto -- yes. Transfer of those citizens from other republics back to the Federative Republic of Serbia, "transfer of," not onto. It would make sense, but when you say "onto," it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you fully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The formulation itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you agree with me, thank you so much, because I think that is what the article is saying, at English version, at least, thereof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not defined properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's fine, but we have agreed. Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you clarify something. Before this order was issued, at the time when the SFRY existed, were certain members of the then JNA also transferred from certain territories to others and why? Can you explain the Court -- to the Court when this happened and what it was?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from the territory of -- territories of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, certain armies were formed. Former members of the JNA joined the ranks of these armies as professional servicemen. Following the transformation of the Yugoslav People's Army into the Army of Yugoslavia, professional soldiers who hailed from these territories, who were born in Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina and happened to be in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia joined these armies of their own free will and thereby left the system of -- the command system of the Army of Yugoslavia and joined the command structure of the other armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to put the question to you again. I may not have made myself quite clear. I was interested in the pre-April 1992 period before the FRY was constituted, and in respect of the JNA within the SFRY was there a time in that period, 1991, when members of the JNA of the old SFRY would be transferred from one territory to the other and why, and what was their status?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to clarify that particular issue and then deal with this one. Their status was not defined at that point in time, and their status was that of members of the Yugoslav People's Army. However, as various armies came into being, the status of these various servicemen who left certain ranks and joined others had to be defined. So in answer to your question, yes, absolutely, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go further, would I like to get what you mean in your question, Mr. Lukic, by the term "territory." You're talking about the territory -- when you say from one territory to another, are you talking about the territory that formed the SFRY or the territory outside the SFRY, because at that time the whole of the SFRY was SFRY territory. Now, when you say "transferred from one territory to another," I'm not sure what you mean, unless you mean a territory outside the SFRY. Greece, Spain --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You -- you're getting close though. The problem lies in me trying to avoid putting leading questions and trying to deal with what was, in fact, a mess, because you had a state called the SFRY without Slovenia being part of it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm using the term "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" but with one part of its former territory outside of it now. So I wanted to skirt the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I fully --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. I fully appreciate that by 1992 Slovenia was out of the federation, and hence my question. Does the word "territory" here refer to what at the beginning of 1992 was the SFRY, in other words, SFRY minus Slovenia; or does it mean territories within the SFRY? Does it mean republics of the SFRY, and all I want to know is what you mean by the word "territories."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I was using what was then the official name, SFRY. Obviously the territory of that country had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what I want to know and I'll try to be more specific with my question is this: Were there any problems with the members of the JNA regarding their status and their position after Slovenia declared its independence in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What exactly was that situation about, something that you would have known of given your line of work at the time?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many members of the JNA, following Slovenia's declaration of independence, as you suggested yourself, and this was later followed by the Republic of Croatia. We are, after all, talking about 1992, the 27th of April, 1992. A time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had already been constituted. As you can tell if you look at this document this refers to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Many of the members had no choice but to leave their flats, take their families with them and physically move them to the territory of the FRY. This caused a lot of social problems. At the time, many of these citizens had not yet resolved issues regarding their nationality or citizenship. I am willing to share with you, if I may, one particular piece of information regarding what the constitution says about this. Following the withdraw of the JNA pursuant to decisions taken at the time by the Presidency of the SFRY, and this is with regard to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as paragraph 2 specifies, 13.000 members arrived from various republics. If my understanding of your question is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thirteen thousand members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke. Members of the JNA with their units and their families on the territory of the FRY with about 40.000 relatives. If I may press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have a problem with the answer. Your question at page 36, starting at line 9, specifically refers to the problems with the members of the JNA regarding their status and their position after Slovenia declared independence. The answer is now dealing with the period after the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina have [indiscernible]. So can you please make sure that you get the witness back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you understand the problem that the Presiding Judge seems to be having with this answer. My question was quite specific. We shall be discussing a wide range of subjects here. I would like you to address my question and no more than my question when you go about answering my questions. What do you know about what the JNA faced after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe say to the witness: After Slovenia broke off but before the break by the other -- by Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to draw a distinction here, and we talked about this during your proofing, sir. This is a long period of time. At one point Slovenia broke off in the summer of 1991. What ramifications did that have vis-a-vis members of the JNA? It's probably best if you answer that question first. With this happening with the cessation or separation or break up of Slovenia from Yugoslavia, in the summer of 1991 that year perhaps and then we can tackle the rest.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To couch this in the briefest possible terms, the most prominent problems arose about the status and position of those members of the JNA, and by the same token there were problems with the records of the military staff withdrawing from the Republic of Slovenia to a different territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a while ago some figures. I'll be asking you about Slovenia in due course, but generally speaking, how did you come to learn about those figures? Did your administration deal with statistics or anything to do with these figures and the records of these persons withdrawing from certain territories in a very general sense?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the analysis that I remember, but don't hold me to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you even start answering, General, my question was: How did you come about that information? Did your administration do that type of work? First let's take this one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset today, I stated that within my administration was also the housing department. One of our basic tasks was to monitor and report on the housing problems and the living standard of these members and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And I'm asking you in terms of specific information, how many professional JNA servicemen left Slovenia's territory, and what were the consequences in terms of the work of your administration?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have specific information regarding Slovenia, but I know how many flats were left in Slovenia. I do have the total figure for Croatia and also for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that gives me something to work on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. One step at a time. Can you tell us about the number of flats that remained in the Republic of Slovenia that used to be JNA property?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analysis was drawn up in 1992. It has been a long time. Therefore, Your Honours, please don't hold me to each and every figure. Nevertheless, I can say that there remained about 6.500 flats in the Republic of Slovenia's territory, and these flats were -- were, before that time, available to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about the Republic of Macedonia? When did Macedonia break off, and what were the consequences regarding members of the JNA, provided your administration was aware of any.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately, an agreement was reached with the Republic of Macedonia, the parties to the agreement being representatives of the federal authorities of the FRY and the representatives of the Republic of Macedonia. A peaceful solution was reached, and there was nothing in the way of peacefully resolving this situation in relation to those members who left the Republic of Macedonia and were now back in the FRY and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What specifically happened with those flats?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite specifically, certain people bought those flats that had previously been owned and used by the JNA. They were now free to exchange those flats with no hindrance whatsoever with those who wished the leave the JNA and join the Army of the Republic of Macedonia. It was up to the persons involved to deal with that and perform these exchanges. Another way was to simply sell the flats off and use any proceeds from those sales in order to buy themselves flats in the FRY, which was definitely an avenue that was open to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In situation number 3, I'm looking at the document in front us, Article 3 specifically, and I'll try to paraphrase this. Acting Federal Secretary Blagoje Adzic would be continuing in keeping with the new constitutional situations and the representatives of all three constituent peoples in that republic. Sir, do you know if any talks were held about the rights of members of the JNA and their status after April 1992, and did that have anything to do with these talks between the three constituent peoples and their political representatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We know what those were.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leaders of the two countries -- rather, the political authorities, as far as I was aware, were in fact having talks, negotiations, in a bid to deal with certain issues regarding the free withdrawal or departure of JNA members, all of them shifting between different armies. They wanted to remove all obstacles to a peaceful progress of this. Opportunities were being seized to make it possible for those people to go wherever they liked with no hindrance at all. I seem to remember that the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army established a team whose task was to monitor the implementation of this plan that was reached. Nevertheless, as far as I know, talks were scheduled to be held by the Acting Federal Secretary for All People's Defence, General Blagoje Adzic, at the time, and I don't think he was successful in agreeing all of the terms for a dignified and peaceful resolution of this problem. Nevertheless, as far as the Army of Yugoslavia was concerned, there was nothing controversial. There were no problems, no members of any other ethnicities were pressured to leave or to stay either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may just latched on to the last thing you were talking about. Do you perhaps know if members of the former JNA who left the JNA and joined, for example, the BH Army or Croatia's army and had flats, for example, in Belgrade, did anyone deny their property rights or take away those flats from them that they happened to own in the territory of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never came across anything like that. I don't think that sort of pressure was ever exerted on any of those individuals as long as they were the rightful owners of those flats, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I see. And what about the flats that happened to be in the Republic of Croatia, for example, in Zagreb or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Sarajevo, flats belonging to members of the JNA who had previously withdrawn from those territories? Were they free to do as they saw fit with those flats? What does your information suggest, sir?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, members of the JNA who were using flats and had tenancy rights, as you pointed out a while ago, but those who bought flats from the JNA, the flats available to the JNA for their use, after the withdrawal of the JNA they were driven out of those flats and were never allowed to use those flats again or indeed to sell those flats in order to try to deal with their own housing issues elsewhere in the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now try to return to what you were talking about earlier on. According to your information, how many members of the JNA came to the FRY from Croatia and how many from Bosnia and Herzegovina and how many relatives? Were any specific records kept?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I talked about the individual figures, the Republic of Slovenia, the Republic of Croatia. I had a collective figure when we drafted this analysis. In our administration our information suggesting at the time that over 13.000 members of the JNA had arrived from these territories followed by another 40.000 relatives. They arrived in the FRY with no accommodation to speak of and nowhere to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would like to intervene. Mr. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just calling your name. I was saying Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Lukic asked you at page 42, line 2: "Were they free to do as they saw fit with those flats? What does your information suggest, sir?" Your answer was: "Regrettably, members of the JNA who were using flats and had tenancy rights, as you pointed out a while ago, but those who bought flats from the JNA, the flats avail --" And you tell us the problems experienced by those in those flats, that they were not allowed to use those flats. You haven't told us what about those who had tenancy rights. Can you tell us what was -- if there was any problem with those who had tenancy rights and if so, what was the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. If I may furnish an additional explanation. As far as I know, after this situation took place, the Croatian parliament adopted a decision for the persons who abandoned their flats and previously had tenancy rights on those flats were to lose those rights and effectively were not able to exercise them any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, on page 42, line 17, you said 13 [as interpreted] members of the JNA. Are you referring to the professional servicemen?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can give you some more information if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I intentionally didn't speak about retired servicemen. To my knowledge and from what I can recall, around 4.000 retired servicemen were expelled from their flats in the above-mentioned republics. That was another problem that the FRY had to resolve, so on top of the 13.000 that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be assigned Exhibit D241. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at another document, Your Honours. The original document is marked P729, but since it's a very bad copy, there's a retyped one produced in the Tribunal. And I think we can talk about Mr. Thomas later about just attaching the B/C/S version to it, and that's a document of the 6th of May, 1992, signed by Blagoje Adzic, and a better copy is 65 ter is 0138D. And the original document is P729, and the original has the seal and the stamp. We are going to look at P729, and you will see how bad the copy is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is a Prosecution exhibit, and I will suggest to you, Mr. Nikolic to look at document 1318D in front of you. Can you find it? Because that's one and the same document?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but just if I may take some time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this document 138D or 1318D?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What you're looking at is 1318D, the 65 ter documents of the Defence. It doesn't have the signature or the stamp, whereas the original version of this document is marked P729.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it. What was your question? I haven't heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, what's the Prosecution's position with respect to the now legible copy that is being produced by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm all in favour of using a copy that is legible. I have no difficulty with the legible copy being attached in some way to the existing exhibit. We have the original already attached which bears the signature and other authenticating features. For the purposes of using the document with General Nikolic, I have no difficulty with the document as suggested by my learned friend being used. I have one qualification. I'm just having somebody check for my own purposes that the -- that the two documents match, but assuming that they do, I ultimately would have no difficulty with this version also being attached to the already tendered exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic -- oh, I'm sorry. I spent a lot of time with another witness. Mr. Nikolic, would you please tell me, are you familiar with this document and what does it speak about?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became familiar with this document during proofing. Since this was written in 1992, I wasn't in the ministry, but I can provide you with very specific and valid answers. The deputy of the federal secretary at the time for national defence colonel-general --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you start, we have to correct a mistake. You said -- I apologise to the interpreters. Page 45, 24 line, the witness said that he was at the ministry at that time.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
